title: Soil morphology

definition.text: The branch of soil science that describes soils technically, above all their physical properties such as texture, colour, structure and consistence.

facts.text: Descriptions are usually made in the field on a profile with several horizons, exposed by digging a pit or taking a core with a push tube or auger.
With soil formation and soil classification, soil morphology is counted as part of pedology, one of the central disciplines of soil science.
Nineteenth-century agro-geologists, who examined soils in natural settings, were the first to study soil morphology scientifically.
Dokuchaev's team saw profiles with similar horizons hundreds of kilometres apart wherever climate and vegetation were similar.
Once soils were seen as independent natural bodies, morphology was used to judge the combined influence of climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time.
Official guidelines for describing soils first appeared in the 1930s, by Charles Kellogg and the USDA Soil Conservation Service in the United States and by G.R. Clarke in the United Kingdom.
A description records site information plus horizons, colour, texture, structure and other properties; many US soil scientists use the USDA-NRCS Pedon Description field sheet.
Structure is described by shape, size and grade, best while the soil is fairly dry, because moist peds swell and press together.

notes: The Color section (Munsell hue, value, chroma) is left to Soil color (reading-a-soil); the Porosity section to the density chapter; the texture methods to the pilot's Texture by feel and Hydrometer method entries.

title: Soil profile

definition.text: A vertical face of soil showing its horizons, layers roughly parallel to the surface; formally, one face of a pedon.

facts.text: Profiles are exposed for study by excavating a pit or by extracting a core with a hand or hydraulic push tube or an auger.
Mature profiles typically have three basic master horizons, A, B and C, but no profile has all the major horizons.
Some soils, such as Entisols, have only one horizon or none, for instance young soils on mine waste, moraines, volcanic cones, dunes or alluvial terraces.
Wind or water erosion can strip the upper horizons, burying them downslope, a natural process that tillage aggravates.
Soils reshaped by major earthworks or regular deep ploughing may lack distinct horizons almost completely.
Going down a profile goes back in time: past events are recorded in horizons much as in sediment layers.
Pollen, testate amoebae and plant remains in horizons can reveal past climate or land-use change, and large charcoal pieces allow radiocarbon dating.

notes: Anchored on the Soil morphology section that defines profile and pedon; several facts come from Soil#Horizons, which the what-soil-is pass may also use.

title: Pedon

definition.text: The imaginary three-dimensional unit of soil large enough to show the full range of properties of a particular soil; a soil profile is one face of it.

facts.text: Pedons generally cover 1 to 10 m2 of land and are the fundamental unit of field soil study.
The Canadian system defines the pedon as a body commonly 1 metre across and 1 to 2 metres deep.
One proposal splits the pedon into a living humipedon, a copedon where most mineral weathering occurs, and a lithopedon in contact with the subsoil.
To classify a soil, every horizon of its pedon is checked against the criteria for diagnostic horizons.

notes: No article; passes the 2+ pages test (Soil morphology, Soil, Canadian system of soil classification, Humus form, Soil horizon).

title: Horizon designation

definition.text: The code of letters and numbers that names each soil horizon: a capital master symbol, often followed by lowercase suffixes, with numbers for discontinuities and subdivisions.

facts.text: A capital letter gives the master horizon, such as O, A, E, B, C or R; lowercase suffixes add details of soil formation.
A numerical prefix marks a lithologic discontinuity, a change in parent material; a numerical suffix splits one horizon into subdivisions such as Bt1, Bt2 and Bt3.
Some master horizons, including O, B and L, must always carry a suffix, and several suffixes may be combined.
The horizons of a profile are joined with hyphens, as in Ah-E-Bt1-2Bt2-2BwC-3C1-3C2.
The notation summarizes colour, size, texture, structure, consistency, roots, pH, voids, boundaries and nodules or concretions.
The same horizon may be labelled differently in different classification systems; there are many systems of horizon symbols in the world.
No system is more correct than another, but because their symbols are defined differently, the systems cannot be mixed.

notes: Soil horizon (reading-a-soil) carries the general notation sentences too; merge if that pass drafts a designation entry.

These numbers follow all the letters. Within a sequence of C horizons, for example, successive horizons may be designated C1, C2, C3, etc. If the lower horizons are strongly gley

definition.text: The lower border of a soil horizon, described in the field by how sharp it is (distinctness) and how its shape varies sideways (topography).

facts.text: Distinctness classes run from very abrupt and abrupt through clear and gradual to diffuse.
Boundaries are often not parallel to the surface and may be broken; topography classes are smooth, wavy, irregular and broken.
Official series descriptions record them, as in the Cecil series: an abrupt smooth boundary below the Ap horizon and gradual wavy boundaries further down.

title: O horizon

definition.text: A surface layer of organic material, built from plant residues not mixed into the mineral soil and not waterlogged for long periods.

facts.text: Organic material is defined by a minimum organic carbon content, 20% by weight in the WRB.
Its residues are typically leaves, conifer needles, twigs, mosses and lichens, partly altered by decomposition.
The upper part is often barely decomposed while the lower part may be strongly humified; the Australian system splits O horizons into O1 and O2 on that basis.
The Australian system keeps the O horizon apart from overlying leaf litter, which has no weathered mineral particles and is not part of the soil.
Organisms living in the O horizon break down organic material and release nutrients, making the soil more active.
Strong acidity, cold or pollution slow decomposition, so undecomposed organic matter builds up in an organic horizon over the mineral soil.
Though formed on top of the mineral soil, O horizons can be buried at depth by landslides, floods or wind-blown dust.
Its upper part is often relatively undecomposed litter, while the lower part may be strongly humified.

notes: All master-horizon entries share the anchor Soil horizon#Master horizons and layers (FAO 2006 section) and draw on the WRB, USDA and Australian sections of the same page.

verification.evidence: The suffix symbols and their meanings follow: a Highly decomposed organic material This symbol is used with O horizons to indicate the most highly decomposed organic materials, which have a fiber content of less than 17 percent (by volume) after rubbing.
verification.note: the Manual's 17% is the fiber content of sapric (highly decomposed) material; the entry gives the WRB's 20% organic carbon threshold for organic material

definition.text: An organic layer, generally peat, that is saturated with water for long periods or has been artificially drained.

facts.text: In the WRB an H layer is saturated for more than 30 consecutive days in most years, or drained; an O horizon is saturated for no more than 30 days and not drained.
Many H horizons consist mainly of sphagnum (peat) mosses.
After drainage, O horizons may form on top of H horizons.
The Australian system calls these waterlogged organic horizons P, for peats, with at least 12 to 18% organic carbon depending on clay content.

title: A horizon

definition.text: The uppermost mineral horizon, at the surface or below an O horizon, where humified organic matter is intimately mixed with mineral material.

facts.text: It is often called topsoil and holds dark decomposed organic matter called humus.
Burrowing animals mix organic matter into the mineral matter there, a process called bioturbation.
Most biological activity happens here: earthworms, potworms, arthropods, nematodes, fungi, bacteria and archaea crowd around plant roots, so it may be called the biomantle.
Because biological activity reaches much deeper, it cannot be the chief test; A horizons are mostly defined relative to the layers beneath.
Original rock structure is fully or largely obliterated in an A horizon.
Layers changed by cultivation or pasturing count as A horizons; the suffix p marks ploughed layers.
The Australian system subdivides it into A1 (dark, most biologically active), A2 (paler) and A3 (transitional to the B horizon).

notes: Topsoil (own article) covers the everyday and agronomic term; this entry is the pedological master horizon.

definition.text: A mineral horizon that has lost clay, iron, aluminium, organic matter or a mix of these, leaving a concentration of sand and silt, mostly quartz.

facts.text: E stands for eluviated: the leached layer is usually pale and made largely of silicates or silica.
It usually lies below an O or A horizon and above a B horizon, from which it differs by higher colour value or lower chroma, coarser texture, or both.
E horizons occur only in older, well-developed soils; pedogenesis there is advanced, since the lost substances first formed or accumulated in place.
The Australian system does not use E; leached layers are labelled A or B with the suffix e.
In gravelly soils, burrowing animals commonly leave a stone layer near or at the base of the E horizon.
Where this eluviation is pronounced, a lighter-coloured E horizon appears below the A horizon.
It is usually, though not always, paler than the B horizon beneath, sometimes taking the colour of its sand and silt particles.
E stands for eluviated; such horizons occur only in older, well-developed soils, generally between the A and B horizons, and the Australian system does not use the symbol.

title: B horizon

definition.text: A subsurface mineral horizon, formed below an A, E, H or O horizon, where the original rock structure is largely gone and soil formation has altered or enriched the material.

facts.text: Commonly called subsoil, it is brownish or reddish from iron oxides, since it holds less organic matter than the A horizon.
Its features include residual oxides or clay minerals, removal of carbonates or gypsum, and illuvial clay, iron, aluminium, organic matter, carbonates, gypsum or silica.
Where it gathers material moving down from the A and E horizons it is also called the illuvial horizon.
The B horizon generally has soil structure, and its structure or consistency differs from the horizons above and below.
Layers with gleying but no other pedogenic change, or with carbonates not contiguous to a genetic horizon above, are not B horizons.
The Australian system splits it into B1 (transitional from A), B2 (concentrated clay or oxides) and B3 (transitional to the C or D horizon).

notes: Subsoil (own article) covers the everyday term; this entry is the pedological master horizon.

definition.text: A layer below the soil horizons, other than hard bedrock, that is little affected by soil formation and lacks the properties of O, A, E or B horizons.

facts.text: It includes sediments, saprolite and soft bedrock that can be dug with a spade when moist and usually slake in water within 24 hours.
C horizons form in deposits such as loess, flood deposits and landslides, or from in-situ weathering of bedrock.
Without a lithologic discontinuity above it, the C horizon resembles the parent material of the solum, though C material may be unlike it.
Plant roots can penetrate C horizons, which form an important growing medium.
It may be enriched with carbonates and other soluble compounds leached down from the solum.
Layers cemented by silica, carbonates or gypsum stay C unless clearly affected by soil formation, when they become B horizons.
It forms either in deposits such as loess, flood deposits or landslides, or by in-situ weathering of residual bedrock.
Where there is no lithologic discontinuity, the C horizon resembles the parent material of the solum above.

definition.text: Hard, consolidated bedrock underlying the soil at the base of the profile.

facts.text: Examples are granite, basalt, quartzite and hard limestone or sandstone; air-dry chunks do not slake in water within 24 hours.
It is too coherent to dig by hand with a spade, and its few small cracks let few roots in.
Where no lithologic discontinuity separates them, the R layer resembles the parent material of the solum.

definition.text: A horizon combining the properties of two master horizons, written with both capital letters, the dominant one first, as in AB or BA.

facts.text: Where separate bodies of two master horizons are intermingled, the symbols are joined with a slash, as in A/B or B/A.
The WRB writes superimposed horizons without a separator, as in AhBw, and uses a slash for separate bodies, as in Bt/E where E material interfingers into a Bt horizon.
The Australian A3, B1 and B3 transitional horizons are loosely defined and used at the describer's discretion.
I, L and W layers are never used in transitional designations.

title: Horizon suffixes

definition.text: Lowercase letters added to a master horizon symbol to record particular features or processes of soil formation.

facts.text: In the USDA field book, t marks illuvial silicate clay, k pedogenic calcium carbonate, g strong gleying and p a plough layer.
Other USDA suffixes include b for a buried genetic horizon, f for permafrost, x for fragipan features and y for gypsum.
WRB letters borrow from other languages: k from German Karbonat, t from German Ton (clay), n from natrium and z from Dutch zout (salt).
Suffixes are combined in order of dominance, as in Btng or Btgb; the cementation suffix m follows the suffix naming the cementing agent.

notes: Anchored on the USDA field book (2024) suffix section; the WRB and FAO suffix lists on the same page differ in detail.

definition.text: A change in parent material within a soil profile, shown in horizon designations by a numerical prefix.

facts.text: By convention the uppermost material carries no number; each lower stratum gets 2, 3 and so on, as in Oi-Oe-Ah-E-2Bt-2C-3R.
Where no discontinuity separates the solum from the C horizon below, that C horizon resembles the solum's parent material.
Numerical suffixes, by contrast, mark subdivisions within a single horizon.

definition.text: A genetic horizon that formed at the surface and was later covered by new mineral material, marked with the suffix b.

facts.text: A fully formed profile may be buried by wind- or water-laid sediments that later form a new profile; this is most common in coastal areas.
Numerical prefixes describe such sequences, as in O, A1, A2, B2, 2A2, 2B21, 2B22, 2C, with the buried profile starting at 2A2.
Fossil soil horizons of paleosols occur within sedimentary rock sequences and record past environments.
Soil formation is often pictured as happening in place, but burial makes the process far more complicated.

definition.text: A horizon defined by a set of criteria, whose presence or absence at a given depth is used to assign soils to taxonomic units.

facts.text: The WRB, USDA soil taxonomy and the Australian Soil Classification pick out diagnostic horizons, whereas the German system defines soils by whole horizon sequences.
Diagnostic horizons usually carry names, such as the cambic or spodic horizon, rather than symbols.
The WRB lists 40 diagnostic horizons.
To classify a soil, each horizon is checked against the criteria, and the soil is allocated from the diagnostic horizons found.
USDA soil taxonomy separates diagnostic surface horizons, the epipedons, from subsurface ones such as the argillic, cambic, spodic and oxic horizons.
Most systems also use soil characteristics other than diagnostic horizons to define taxonomic units.

title: Epipedon

definition.text: In USDA soil taxonomy, a diagnostic surface horizon, the upper part of the soil.

facts.text: The USDA epipedons are the anthropic, folistic, histic, melanic, mollic, ochric, plaggen and umbric epipedons.
A fertile mollic epipedon, built by long additions of root-derived organic matter, is the defining feature of Mollisols.
Histosols must have a histic epipedon; an ochric epipedon is common in Entisols and Aridisols.
Inceptisols usually have an ochric or umbric epipedon over a cambic horizon; plaggen or anthropic epipedons signal intense, prolonged human activity.

notes: No article; mentioned on Soil horizon, USDA soil taxonomy, Mollisol, Inceptisol, Argillic and Olympic (soil).

title: Albic horizon

definition.text: A bleached, light-coloured subsurface diagnostic horizon left when soil formation moves clay minerals and oxides downward.

facts.text: It is a diagnostic horizon in both the WRB and USDA soil taxonomy.
Spodosols, acidic soils common in coniferous and boreal forests, usually have an albic horizon.
In Albeluvisols the albic horizon tongues into a clay-illuvial Bt horizon; in Stagnosols the topsoil can be completely bleached.
Plinthosols often show eluviation as an albic horizon beneath an umbric surface layer.

notes: No article; passes the 2+ pages test (Soil horizon, USDA soil taxonomy, WRB, Albeluvisols, Stagnosol, Plinthosol, Cambic horizon).

title: Topsoil

definition.text: The upper layer of soil, richest in organic matter and microorganisms, where most of the soil's biological activity takes place.

facts.text: A mix of mineral particles and organic matter usually 5–10 inches (13–25 cm) deep, it holds water and air that encourage biological activity.
Roots concentrate in topsoil, where plants obtain most of their nutrients; bacteria and fungi break down organic matter and insects aerate and turn the soil.
Its depth is measured from the surface to the first densely packed layer, the subsoil; classification systems call it the O or A horizon.
More organic matter strengthens soil structure; dried-out topsoil loses much of its volume and becomes more prone to wind erosion.
An optimum carbon-to-nitrogen ratio for UK topsoil is less than 20:1.
One inch (2.5 cm) of topsoil can take 500 to 1,000 years to form, and current use and erosion outpace soil generation.
The United States loses almost 3 tons of topsoil per acre per year.
Cover crops, crop rotation, conservation tillage and windbreaks are used to slow erosion and keep topsoil fertile.

notes: S:87ec45b72b1a (about 60 years of topsoil left, on 2014 trends) was left out; the verification pass may want to look at it.

definition.text: Soil mixtures sold as topsoil, either natural topsoil mined and conditioned for use or manufactured from minerals, biosolids, compost or paper mill sludge.

facts.text: It is used to improve gardens and lawns, fill containers and grade the ground around buildings, but suits potting less well than potting soil or compost.
In the UK it must be classified under British Standard BS 3882 (2015), with thresholds for nutrients, phytotoxic elements, particle size, organic matter, pH and contamination.
The United States has no federal legal definition of topsoil sold in commerce.
Artificial growing media include terra preta and potting mix; low-quality artificial topsoil helped rehabilitate an open-cut coal mine in Victoria, Australia.

definition.text: The layer of soil beneath the topsoil, a mix of sand, silt and clay with much less organic matter and humus.

facts.text: Most soil mapping systems label it the B horizon; below it lies the substratum or C horizon.
With little organic matter, its colour comes mainly from iron oxides.
Rain carries weathering products such as clay minerals and iron oxides down as solutes and colloids, and they accumulate in the subsoil, the depth of most deposition.
Physical, chemical and biological activity give the subsoil a soil structure, which sets it apart from the substratum below.
Though not sterile, it holds few soil organisms compared with humus-rich topsoil.
Human activity has mixed topsoil and subsoil in many environments.
Clay-rich subsoil has supplied adobe, cob, rammed earth and wattle and daub for millennia.

definition.text: The upper part of a soil, its surface and subsoil layers, that has developed under the same soil-forming conditions.

facts.text: In horizon terms it is the A, E and B horizons, their transitional horizons and some O horizons; its base is relatively unweathered parent material.
It includes horizons of carbonate or salt accumulation if they formed at least partly in the same period of soil formation.
A solum has no minimum or maximum thickness: a 10 cm surface layer on bedrock can be the whole solum, while fresh alluvium has none.
Its lower limit should relate to the rooting depth expected for perennial plants, though in some soils it can only be set arbitrarily.
Hardened carbonate or gleying many metres down is hard to count as solum, since deep features may be relict or geological rather than pedological.
The living part of the soil is largely confined to the solum and is most prominent in the A horizon.

verification.evidence: An A horizon that is 10 cm thick overlying bedrock is by itself the solum.

title: Hardpan

definition.text: A dense, largely water-impervious soil layer, usually lying just below the topsoil.

facts.text: Some pans form when deposits such as dissolved silica, iron oxides or calcium carbonate fuse and bind the soil particles.
Others are man-made, compacted by repeated ploughing, especially with moldboard ploughs, by heavy traffic or by pollution.
Acidic soils are most affected, because iron and calcium salts form hard complexes with soil particles under acid conditions.
Clay-rich soils compact easily, and sodium in wastewater can bind clay into a local hardpan, a common cause of septic system failure.
Hardpans impede drainage and restrict root growth on farms and in gardens.
They can be broken mechanically with a broadfork, digging fork or spade, or with a tractor-drawn chisel plough.
Manure, compost or peat improve drainage and encourage earthworms that slowly break pans; lime and gypsum help with harder pans, but amendments may take years.
Plinthite turns irreversibly into an ironstone hardpan when exposed to repeated wetting and drying.

notes: The plough pan or tillage pan (Plough, Tillage pages) is folded in as the man-made kind.

definition.text: A dense, compact, slowly permeable subsoil layer with much more clay than the material above, from which a sharp boundary separates it.

facts.text: Its dense structure restricts roots and water infiltration, so a perched water table can form on top of it.
The Canadian system defines claypan as a clay-enriched illuvial B (Bt) horizon.
It covers about 4 million ha of the central United States, in states such as Kansas, Oklahoma and Illinois, and also occurs in south-west Queensland.
Bare ground, particle-size distribution and heavy rain favour it: raindrops rearrange fine sand, silt and clay until they plug the pores into a packed layer.
Dominated by montmorillonite, it shrinks hard in the dry season and swells wet and sticky in the wet season, with poor aeration.
It holds much water, but most is unavailable to plants because it evaporates and the pores are tiny.
Acidic and clay-rich, it binds phosphorus so tightly that much P fertilizer is needed, while its potassium stays available to plants.
Slow infiltration and perched water increase surface runoff, leaving claypan soils highly vulnerable to erosion of the organic-rich topsoil.

definition.text: A diagnostic horizon of USDA soil taxonomy in which illuvial silica has cemented the subsoil into a hardpan.

facts.text: It is usually written Bqm; the closest Canadian equivalent is the duric horizon, and the WRB counterpart is the petroduric horizon.
Duripans form almost only in arid or Mediterranean climates and can be as hard as concrete, so their soils are seldom cultivated and mostly used for grazing or wildlife.
Silica from fast-weathering volcanic glass, or from iron-magnesium minerals and feldspars, is carried into the subsoil and precipitates as microaggregates that grow into a pan.
Criteria include cementation of over half the volume, roots only along fractures 10 cm or more apart, and slaking in KOH but not HCl, which separates it from petrocalcic horizons and fragipans.

title: Fragipan

definition.text: A diagnostic horizon of USDA soil taxonomy: an altered, dense subsurface layer that restricts water flow and root penetration.

facts.text: It is written Bx or Btx and limits land use much as a duripan does; the WRB counterpart is the fragic horizon.
Fragipans are firm and brittle near field capacity with virtually no roots, yet air-dry fragments slake in water, unlike duripans and petrocalcic horizons.
They contain no calcium or magnesium carbonate and do not effervesce in dilute HCl.
Proposed origins include glacial compaction, permafrost, physical ripening, inheritance from paleosols, and hydroconsolidation, the collapse of structure under loading and wetting.

contested_note: Soil scientists debate how fragipans form, how to define them and whether they exist in certain landscapes (S:85fb395526b9, S:3fc191113f55).

definition.text: A diagnostic horizon of USDA soil taxonomy and the WRB in which secondary carbonates have cemented the subsoil into a hardpan.

facts.text: It is cemented by carbonates, with or without silica, and roots get through only along vertical fractures 10 cm or more apart.
Carbonates from parent material or dust are carried down by water and precipitate as it evaporates, building a massive, continuous cemented layer.
It marks advanced soil evolution in older soils, and most formed before the Holocene.
Carbonates typify alkaline soils of arid and semiarid climates and are detected in the field by fizzing with hydrochloric acid.

definition.text: A thick, dark, organic-rich surface horizon that is acid and low in bases; its name comes from Latin umbra, shade.

facts.text: It normally has a pH below 5.5 and a base saturation under 50 percent.
WRB criteria include Munsell chroma and value of 3 or less when moist, at least 0.6% organic carbon, and a thickness of at least 100 mm on hard rock, otherwise 200 mm.
Roots growing horizontally can indicate its acidity.
Similar dark, base-poor horizons made by deep cultivation, kitchen middens or manuring are told apart by artifacts, spade marks or land-use history.

definition.text: A diagnostic subsurface horizon showing early pedogenic change, recognized when it does not meet the requirements of any other diagnostic horizon.

facts.text: It lacks appreciable illuviated clay, organic carbon, iron and aluminium oxyhydroxides, carbonate, gypsum or soluble salts.
Its texture must be no coarser than loamy fine sand or very fine sand.
It is commonest in Mollisols and Inceptisols, and also occurs in Andisols, designated Bw or Bg.
With less clay than an argillic horizon, it develops into an argillic (Bt) horizon once the soil becomes an Alfisol along a chronosequence.

definition.text: The deposition in a lower soil layer of material, called illuvium, washed down by rainwater from a layer above.

facts.text: Removal of material from a layer is eluviation; illuviation is the matching build-up further down.
Illuvium includes organic matter, silicate clay and hydrous oxides of iron and aluminium, which collect in subsoil B horizons, the zones of illuviation.
Transport is basically vertical, unlike alluviation, the horizontal transfer by running water.
In mechanical illuviation, a drier horizon draws water from percolating suspensions by capillarity, leaving fine coatings called cutans along the channels.
In chemical illuviation, dissolved constituents carried by leaching are deposited where soil chemistry, especially pH and redox potential, changes.
Clay skins are called argillans, and horizons with enough illuvial clay are argillic horizons.
In medium-textured soils, clay is often washed down the profile and accumulates in the subsoil.

title: Eluviation

definition.text: The removal of soil material from upper layers by water percolating down through the profile.

facts.text: Eluviation occurs when precipitation exceeds evaporation.
A horizon formed by it is an eluvial horizon; some sources count both the A and the E horizon as the eluvial zone.
It moves mineral and organic colloids, which sets it apart from leaching, a distinct mechanism of soil formation.
On a slope, upper facets lose salts by eluviation while lower facets gain them by illuviation.
Organic acids in acid conditions make iron and aluminium more soluble and enhance eluviation; podsolisation is an extreme case that removes iron and aluminium sesquioxides.
The material builds up lower in the profile as an illuvial deposit, a process called illuviation.
It occurs where precipitation exceeds evaporation.
It forms an eluvial horizon: a light-coloured zone at the base of the A horizon (Ae) or a separate E horizon below it, where the process is most intense.

notes: No article of its own: Eluvium (weathering-and-parent-material seed) is mainly the deposit. Leaching (pedology), Cheluviation and Podsolisation are how-soils-form seeds.; Eluvium's lead (S:386c5fcc8d50) calls the removal process 'eluviation or leaching', while Leaching (pedology) (S:ab880751572b) treats the two as distinct; the facts follow the distinction. horizons-and-the-soil-profile also drafts Eluviation (no article); merge, keeping the Eluvium anchor.

definition.text: Frost churning: the mixing of material from different soil horizons, down to bedrock, by repeated freezing and thawing in permafrost soils.

facts.text: It occurs to some degree in most Gelisols, whose name comes from Latin gelare, to freeze.
Autumn freezing forms ice wedges in the most erodible parts of the parent rock; in summer the active layer lets loosened material move both down and up.
Moisture moves from the warm surface to the cold permafrost table, drying the upper soil into a granular structure with ice lenses.
Separation of coarse from fine material produces patterned ground.
It is strongest on exposed sites and weak in sheltered valleys: Turbels show it in over one-third of the active layer, with distorted horizon boundaries, Orthels in less.
It is the dominant force in the active layer and tends to make it uniform in composition.
In frost boils it can bring base-rich water up to the surface, neutralizing acidity and replenishing nutrients.
Ice lenses grow by drawing unfrozen water along a thermal gradient, displacing and mixing mineral and organic material at the ice-water interface.

sources.title: 1.2: Soil Genesis - Geosciences LibreTexts (Digging into Canadian Soils)

definition.text: A Mexican term, from Nahuatl tepetlatl, for a horizon hardened by compaction or cementation in volcanic regions of Mexico.

facts.text: At the surface, tepetates are hard, poorly drained and infertile, which makes them a problem for farming.
Buried under soil, they raise the risk of erosion and landslides because water runs off sideways instead of soaking in.

title: Ice wedge

definition.text: A crack in the ground holding a narrow wedge of ice up to 3–4 metres long at the surface and reaching several metres down.

facts.text: By the widely accepted thermal contraction theory, winter cold opens cracks a few cm wide that fill with snowmelt, freeze, and crack again each winter.
A mean annual air temperature of −6 to −8 °C or colder is thought necessary, and the wedges usually form polygonal patterns.
Epigenetic wedges grow in existing permafrost, widening to 3–5 m; syngenetic wedges grow upward as sediment accumulates and can reach 25 m deep.
Where permafrost has gone, melted wedges fill with sediment; these ice wedge casts help estimate climates of hundreds of thousands of years ago.

notes: Assigned by the concept graph; the cryoturbation link places it in the profile chapter. The cited −17 °C cracking threshold (S:6f6518533dbc) carries a citation-needed tag and was not used.

title: Cecil (soil)

definition.text: A soil series of the south-eastern US Piedmont, a fine, kaolinitic Ultisol first mapped in Cecil County, Maryland, in 1899.

facts.text: More than 10 million acres (40,000 km2) are mapped, and Cecil is North Carolina's state soil.
Formed over granite and chemically similar rocks, it has a brown sandy loam topsoil over red, kaolinite-rich clay subsoil with mica.
Its official profile runs Ap, Bt1, Bt2, BC and C, the C being loam saprolite, with clay films on ped faces in the Bt horizons.
Erosion has stripped the topsoil from many cultivated areas, exposing the red clay subsoil; like other kaolinitic clays it barely recovers from compaction.

notes: Kept as a worked example of an official profile description. S:d3da99dd2549 (state soil, range) is flagged as an irrelevant citation; the state-soil fact cites the List of U.S. state soils row instead.; curriculum review: a single soil series

definition.text: A hard, erosion-resistant layer of sedimentary rock, usually conglomerate or breccia, cemented into a duricrust by iron oxides.

facts.text: The iron oxide cement comes from the oxidation of percolating iron-salt solutions; the name joins ferruginous and concrete.
It forms at or near the land surface and may hold sediments brought from elsewhere; synonyms include ferruginous duricrust, hardpan and ironpan.
Some laterites contain ferricrete, which has been suggested to form in their wetter, leached parts.
In rural South Africa it is widely used to build roads and is known by its Afrikaans name koffieklip, coffee stone.

title: Cob (material)

definition.text: A natural building material made from subsoil, water, fibrous organic material such as straw, and sometimes lime.

facts.text: Subsoil lacking the right mix is adjusted with sand or clay; cob walls need 30% or more clay in the soil.
Cob is fireproof, termite-proof and resistant to earthquakes, but very labour-intensive.
Used for building since prehistoric times, it has been used in Iran for more than 4000 years.

notes: Assigned by the concept graph through its subsoil link. Excluded: an earthen building material, outside a soil science course (the pilot skipped Loam's building uses for the same reason).

definition.text: A former class of the zonal soil order: soils of semiarid and arid regions rich in calcium carbonate and low in organic matter.

facts.text: Under a thin A horizon, calcite and other soluble minerals that water would normally remove build up in the B horizon as a cemented layer, caliche.
Marbut's classification split soils at its highest level into pedocals and pedalfers, the latter rich in aluminium and iron.
The term is not used in the current US classification but often appears in college geology texts.

title: Olympic (soil)

definition.text: A deep, dark reddish-brown, moderately fine-textured soil series formed on mafic rock such as basalt in south-western Washington and western Oregon.

facts.text: Its pedon has an umbric epipedon to 13 inches over an argillic horizon from 13 to 100 inches, in a solum 60 to more than 100 inches thick.
Below a shallow topsoil come five Bt horizons with illuvial clay, the pH falling from 5.8 in the Bt1 to 4.8 in the Cr horizon of weathered basalt.
These fertile soils are used mostly for forestry; high clay in the Bt horizons makes them prone to compaction.
Formerly classed as Xeric Haplohumults, they resemble Alfisols, and Luvisols in the Canadian system.

notes: Kept as a second worked profile example (with Cecil); selection may drop one.; curriculum review: a single soil series

definition.text: A hard soil duricrust formed when surface soil, sand and gravel are cemented by dissolved silica.

facts.text: It forms in a similar way to calcrete, cemented by calcium carbonate, and ferricrete, cemented by iron oxide, and looks like quartzite.
Microcrystalline silcretes form in arid settings with rising pH and lacustrine silcretes where pH falls; silcrete often caps landforms in arid Australia and Africa.
Aboriginal Australians and Middle Stone Age Africans prized silcrete for tools, heat-treating it to flake more easily, possibly the first use of pyrotechnology.
At Pinnacle Point in South Africa, heat-treated silcrete tools date to between 60,000 and 80,000 years ago.

definition.text: Changes in soil texture or structure at natural surfaces of particles, pores or peds, caused by illuviation.

facts.text: They are oriented deposits of any soil component: clay skins or coatings of silica, sesquioxides, manganese, organic matter or carbonate.
Clay skins are also called argillans; a horizon with enough clay illuviation is an argillic horizon.
Visible in the field, they show the degree and nature of soil formation, and reading them is a core skill in soil morphology and paleopedology.
Clay cutans show lineations from oriented clay under cross-polarized light and survive in paleosols after the original voids are lost, making them one of the most diagnostic paleosol features.

definition.text: A weathered layer of bedrock.

facts.text: The name comes from the Greek para, "akin to", and lithic, "stony".
A paralithic contact is one of the depth limits used to define soil classes, as in the definitions of the Gelisol suborders.

definition.text: In pedology, the polished surfaces of cracks that form in soils with a high proportion of swelling clays.

facts.text: Slickensides are a type of cutan.
In the Australian Soil Classification, slickensides with lenticular aggregates indicate a vertisol.
In geology the name is given to fault surfaces smoothed by friction and striated in the direction of movement.

title: Spodic horizon

definition.text: An iron-rich diagnostic subsurface horizon of podzols, where iron and aluminium oxides accumulate with humus.

facts.text: Spodosols must have a spodic horizon within 2 m of the surface, usually under an albic horizon; they are acidic soils of coniferous and boreal forests.
It is a diagnostic horizon in both the WRB and USDA soil taxonomy.
The Polish classification uses it to define the order of soils formed mainly by podzolisation.

notes: Phrase concept, no article; mentioned on Soil horizon, USDA soil taxonomy, Brown podzolic, Polish Soil Classification and Argillic.

title: Mollic epipedon

definition.text: The fertile, dark surface horizon that is the defining diagnostic feature of Mollisols.

facts.text: It builds up through long-term additions of organic matter from plant roots and typically has soft, granular structure.
Mollisols must have one and a base saturation above 50%; they are common in grasslands.
Where shrink–swell clays dominate, a soil with a mollic epipedon is classed a Vertisol; in Andisols the andic properties take precedence.
Greyzems combine a mollic horizon with dry-forest vegetation, where organic accumulation outweighs leaching.

notes: Phrase concept, no article; mentioned on Mollisol, USDA soil taxonomy, Houdek (soil) and Greyzem.

title: Natric horizon

definition.text: An argillic horizon in which large amounts of exchangeable sodium have accumulated.

facts.text: Solonetz soils have a natric horizon within the upper 100 cm; the name comes from natrium, Latin for sodium.
Alfisols and Mollisols with a natric horizon belong mainly to the Solonetz.
It develops from an argillic horizon and is a diagnostic horizon in both the WRB and USDA soil taxonomy.

notes: Phrase concept, no article; mentioned on Argillic, Solonetz, Alfisol, Mollisol and USDA soil taxonomy.

title: Kandic horizon

definition.text: An argillic horizon whose clays are mainly 1:1 silicate clays, giving it a low cation exchange capacity.

facts.text: Because of its low cation exchange capacity it stores nutrients poorly.
Alfisols must have an argillic, natric or kandic horizon, and Ultisols an argillic or kandic one.
Nitisols correspond to kandic Alfisols, Ultisols and Inceptisols, and Acrisols partly to Oxisols with a kandic horizon.

notes: Phrase concept, no article; mentioned on Argillic, USDA soil taxonomy, Nitisol, Acrisol and Soil horizon.

title: Calcic horizon

definition.text: A horizon of secondary carbonate accumulation, above 15% calcium carbonate equivalent and at least 5% more carbonate than the layer below.

facts.text: Calcids have a calcic, hypercalcic or petrocalcic horizon whose upper boundary lies within 1.0 m of the surface.
Calciorthids, Aridisols of the U.S. Soil Taxonomy, are distinguished by a calcic horizon; most Ustolls also have one.
Aridisols have been redefined as soils with a calcic horizon less than 1 meter deep.

notes: Phrase concept, no article; mentioned on Calcareous, Calcid, Calciorthid, Ustic, Paleopedology and Haplocambids.

title: Soil monolith

definition.text: A soil profile dug from the ground in one piece, without disturbing its layers, and preserved for study or display.

facts.text: Each monolith is processed for a month or longer before it is mounted for museum display.
The World Soil Museum shows some 80 monoliths and stores about 1000 from over 70 countries, each with site data and horizon-by-horizon descriptions.
The Dokuchaev Central Museum of Soil holds about 330 monoliths representing the world's soil diversity.

notes: Phrase concept, no article; mentioned on World Soil Museum, Dokuchaev Central Museum of Soil, Kerala Soil Museum, Menfro, Humus form and Lysimeter.
